newsitem.title: JAPAN: Deregulation seen only Japan card in US trade game.
newsitem.headline: Deregulation seen only Japan card in US trade game.

text.p: Promises to cut the red tape that stifles imports and growth may be all Japanese leaders have to offer when U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin comes to seek assurances Tokyo will not let its trade surplus swell.
Rubin is expected to urge Japan not to export its way out of economic trouble and to adopt policies to ensure domestic growth when he meets Japanese leaders here on Friday.

Rubin's visit, during which he will meet Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, is of keen concern to markets seeking clues to whether Washington's tolerance for a strong dollar is waning.

U.S. officials including Rubin have issued increasingly loud warnings to Tokyo not to let its trade surplus balloon again -- a prospect economists say is a likely outcome of Washington's own policy in favour of a strong dollar.
"They have made real progress (in cutting their trade surplus), but the issue is not to have it go back the other way," Rubin said in Washington on Tuesday.
Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus rose 6.5 percent in February from a year earlier, its first jump in over two years. Its surplus with the United States grew 12.3 percent.

Tokyo policy-makers have insisted Japan's recovery is on track, that its surplus is not poised to grow substantially and that priority must be given to cutting its big budget deficit rather than stimulating growth with public spending.

A key Bank of Japan survey released on Wednesday, however, showed that manufacturers were doing well in large part due to the boost to exports from the weak yen. A central bank official said that while the economy was still improving, a consumption tax rise from April 1, recent weak share prices, fiscal tightening and various structural reforms were clouding the business outlook.
Japan's tight fiscal stance and its already rock-bottom interest rates mean deregulation is pretty much Tokyo's sole option to reply to Rubin's concerns, economists said.

"Japan's fiscal situation is tight and...there is not much scope to take new measures such as suggested by (U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Larry) Summers," said Yasunori Miwa, an economist at Itochu Corp. "But they could move ahead rapidly with deregulation."

That stance may gain some sympathy from Rubin and company, but how much remains to be seen. "The political fallout (from the trade issue) has been limited to the auto industry," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.

"Second, the rise in the surplus is pretty much if not largely a consequence of Rubin's own strong dollar policy. They know that in terms of macropolicy Japan is unwilling or unable to do anything about it," he added.
U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich on Tuesday urged Japan not to seek to solve its problems through "lax monetary or fiscal policy" but to take bolder steps to deregulate.
U.S. officials as well as analysts have been lukewarm to Japanese deregulation steps announced thus far, including the final update of a three-year plan released last week.
"Certainly, the foreign view is that the speed and scope of deregulation is inadequate," Miwa said.
Japanese officials may also indicate willingness to take fiscal steps later in the year should their optimism about the recovery prove unfounded, some economists said.

"What they can agree to is that if information over the next few months suggests the U.S. is right and Japan wrong, they might take action," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

Japanese officials are also expected to reassure Rubin that the nation's banking system is sound following Tuesday's announcement of a plan to restructure Nippon Credit Bank, one of the nation's wobbliest banks, and another to merge troubled Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd with rival bank Hokkaido Bank Ltd.

But convincing Rubin that assessment is correct could have some unwelcome fallout, said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities (Japan). "One of the reasons the United States has been holding fire (on trade) is its fears about Japan's financial system," Jerram said.
